senses.gloss: Made to be chewed before swallowing, not swallowed whole.
examples: The kids take *chewable* vitamins every morning.
Are these allergy tablets *chewable*, or do I swallow them?
The pharmacist gave me a *chewable* form of the medicine.

senses.gloss: Needing a lot of chewing; soft but firm or sticky.
examples: I like my chocolate chip cookies soft and *chewy*.
The steak was dry and *chewy*.
This bagel is *chewier* than the ones from the other bakery.

contrast: Pronounced SHEEK, not like *chick*. *Chic* means elegant in a fashionable, understated way; Russian *шикарный* can also mean luxurious and showy, which is closer to *lavish* or *flashy*.

senses.gloss: Fashionable and elegant in style.
examples: She always looks *chic*, even in jeans.
They opened a *chic* little wine bar downtown.
The new lobby is much more *chic* than the old one.

position: predicative only — never before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more chicken*; usually *too chicken* or *so chicken*
contrast: In *chicken soup* or *chicken wings*, *chicken* is a noun used as a modifier, not this adjective. The verb phrase *chicken out* means to lose your nerve (*He chickened out at the last minute*), and the noun works too: *You're such a chicken!*

senses.gloss: Afraid to do something; cowardly.
examples: Come on, jump in — don't be *chicken*!
I was too *chicken* to ask her out.
Everyone knew he was *chicken* when it came to roller coasters.

senses.gloss: Built around children's needs and interests rather than adults' plans.
examples: The school takes a *child-centered* approach to learning.
Our pediatrician's office is very *child-centered*.
Parenting has become far more *child-centered* than it was fifty years ago.

senses.gloss: Having no children.
examples: They were a *childless* couple in their forties.
She stayed *childless* by choice.
The survey compared parents with *childless* adults.

contrast: Always a capital *C*, unlike Russian *чилийский*. It is also a noun: *a Chilean*. Some Americans say chi-LAY-uhn, closer to Spanish.

senses.gloss: Of or from Chile, its people or its culture.
examples: We had a bottle of *Chilean* wine with dinner.
Her husband is *Chilean*.
The *Chilean* coastline stretches for thousands of miles.

contrast: *Chilling* frightens you; *chilled* means made cold (*chilled wine*). In slang, *We're just chilling* is the verb *chill*, meaning relaxing, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Frightening, especially in a cold, quiet way.
examples: The movie tells a *chilling* story about a small-town murder.
His calm description of the crime was *chilling*.
The most *chilling* part was the silence afterward.

senses.gloss: Making people afraid to act or speak freely; used mainly in *a chilling effect*.
examples: Critics say the new law will have a *chilling* effect on free speech.
The lawsuits had a *chilling* effect on reporters.

senses.gloss: Cheap-looking and poorly made.
examples: The hotel room had *chintzy* plastic furniture.
That trophy looks kind of *chintzy*.
They put up the *chintziest* decorations I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to spend money; stingy.
examples: Don't be *chintzy* — leave a decent tip.
The company has always been *chintzy* about raises.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and full of energy.
examples: You're awfully *chipper* for seven in the morning.
She sounded *chipper* on the phone.
He seemed a lot more *chipper* after his nap.

form: -y from *chirp*, a bird's short high sound

senses.gloss: Cheerful and lively, sometimes a little too bright.
examples: The receptionist was annoyingly *chirpy*.
She left a *chirpy* message on my voicemail.
He's always *chirpier* after his first cup of coffee.

form: -ed from *chisel*, a tool for cutting stone or wood
contrast: American spelling has one *l*: *chiseled*. *Chiselled* is British.

senses.gloss: Having strong, sharp, clearly defined lines, especially of a face or muscles.
examples: The actor is known for his *chiseled* jaw.
His arms looked *chiseled* after months at the gym.
She has high, *chiseled* cheekbones.

contrast: It starts with a *sh* sound, not *ch*.

senses.gloss: Polite, kind and protective, especially of a man toward women.
examples: It was *chivalrous* of him to give up his seat.
He made a *chivalrous* offer to walk her home.
Some women find the gesture *chivalrous*; others find it old-fashioned.

position: predicative only — or right after a noun: *a book chock-full of ideas*

senses.gloss: Completely full; packed.
examples: The fridge is *chock-full* of leftovers.
Her essay was *chock-full* of typos.
It's a guidebook *chock-full* of useful tips.

contrast: Usually a noun (*make a choice*). The adjective goes only before a noun and sounds a little formal, except in *a few choice words*, which means angry or rude words, not carefully chosen polite ones.

senses.gloss: Of very high quality; carefully picked as the best.
examples: The butcher saves the *choicest* cuts for his regular customers.
We got *choice* seats near the stage.
The lake has some *choice* spots for fishing.

senses.gloss: Angry or rude; used mainly in *a few choice words*.
examples: He had a few *choice* words for the referee.
When she saw the bill, she used some *choice* language.

senses.gloss: Very careful about what you choose; hard to please.
examples: She's *choosy* about the guys she dates.
He's a *choosy* eater, so we never go anywhere new.
Cats are often *choosier* about food than dogs.

senses.gloss: Cut into small pieces with a knife.
examples: Add a cup of *chopped* onions.
Top the salad with *chopped* walnuts.
Make sure the garlic is finely *chopped*.

senses.gloss: Of water: rough, with many small waves.
examples: The lake was too *choppy* for kayaking.
We hit *choppy* water on the way back.
The bay gets *choppier* in the afternoon.

senses.gloss: Not smooth; broken into short, jerky parts.
examples: The video call was *choppy*, so I couldn't hear her.
His writing is *choppy*, with lots of short sentences.

contrast: The *ch* is a *k* sound, and in American English *choral* sounds the same as *coral*.

senses.gloss: For or sung by a choir.
examples: She directs the *choral* program at the high school.
They performed a *choral* version of the hymn.
The concert features *choral* music from the 1700s.

contrast: British informal *chronic* meaning 'very bad' (*The food was chronic*) is not used in American English.

senses.gloss: Of an illness or pain: lasting a long time or keeping coming back.
examples: She has suffered from *chronic* back pain for years.
Diabetes is a *chronic* disease.
His cough eventually became *chronic*.

senses.gloss: Of a problem or habit: always happening; habitual.
examples: The city has a *chronic* shortage of affordable housing.
He's a *chronic* liar.
*Chronic* lateness got her fired.

senses.gloss: Arranged in the order in which events happened.
examples: List your jobs in reverse *chronological* order.
The museum tells the city's story in *chronological* order.
The novel's timeline isn't strictly *chronological*.

contrast: Friendly when said about babies and cheeks; about an adult it can sound rude. The neutral words are *heavy* and *overweight*.

senses.gloss: Slightly fat, in a round and often cute way.
examples: Look at the baby's *chubby* little cheeks!
I was a *chubby* kid, but I grew out of it.
Our cat has gotten *chubbier* since we moved.

form: -y from *chum*, an old word for a friend

senses.gloss: Very friendly, sometimes too friendly.
examples: He's gotten pretty *chummy* with the boss.
The two senators seemed awfully *chummy* at dinner.
They're *chummier* now than they were in college.

senses.gloss: Thick, heavy and solid-looking.
examples: She wore a *chunky* knit sweater.
*Chunky* gold necklaces are back in style.
These boots have a *chunkier* heel.

senses.gloss: Of food: containing pieces rather than smooth.
examples: Do you like smooth or *chunky* peanut butter?
The salsa is nice and *chunky*.

senses.gloss: Of a person or animal: short, broad and a little heavy.
examples: He was a *chunky* linebacker from Ohio.
Our dog is a *chunky* little beagle.

senses.gloss: Going to church regularly.
examples: She grew up in a *churchgoing* family in Georgia.
The town is small and mostly *churchgoing*.
*Churchgoing* Americans are less common than they were in the 1970s.

takes: *to*-infinitive, mainly in *It would be churlish to...*
form: -ish from *churl*, an old word for a rude man

senses.gloss: Rude and unfriendly, especially when you ought to be grateful or polite.
examples: It would be *churlish* to complain about a free meal.
He gave a *churlish* reply and walked away.
Refusing their invitation seemed *churlish*.

comparison: more/most — *more cinematic* in the 'like a movie' sense; the first sense is not gradable

senses.gloss: Relating to movies and moviemaking.
examples: Hitchcock's *cinematic* techniques are still studied today.
It was her first *cinematic* role.

senses.gloss: Looking or feeling like a movie; dramatic and visual.
examples: The video game has *cinematic* graphics.
The new season feels even more *cinematic* than the last.
Her novels are so *cinematic* that they read like screenplays.

senses.gloss: Relating to the body's natural 24-hour cycle.
examples: Jet lag throws off your *circadian* rhythm.
Blue light at night can disrupt *circadian* cycles.
Scientists study the *circadian* clock in fruit flies.

senses.gloss: Long and indirect; not going straight to a place or to the point.
examples: We took a *circuitous* route to avoid traffic.
His explanation was long and *circuitous*.
The trail to the summit is more *circuitous* than it looks on the map.

senses.gloss: Relating to the movement of blood through the body.
examples: The heart is the center of the *circulatory* system.
Smoking can cause *circulatory* problems.
He has a rare *circulatory* disorder.

senses.gloss: Careful not to take risks or say too much.
examples: The senator was *circumspect* about her plans.
Investors have become more *circumspect* since the crash.
He gave a *circumspect* answer.

senses.gloss: Based on facts that suggest something is true but do not prove it directly.
examples: The case against him was purely *circumstantial*.
Prosecutors relied on *circumstantial* evidence.
The jury convicted her on *circumstantial* evidence alone.

contrast: Also an adverb: *The ban applies citywide*.

senses.gloss: Covering or happening in the whole city.
examples: The mayor announced a *citywide* curfew.
There was a *citywide* power outage last night.
The recycling program is now *citywide*.

contrast: *Civic* is about a citizen's part in the life of a town or country (*civic duty*, *civic pride*). *Civil* is about citizens as opposed to the military or the church, and also means polite (*civil rights*, *a civil answer*). *Civilian* means not in the armed forces (*civilian clothes*).

senses.gloss: Relating to the duties and activities of citizens.
examples: Voting is a *civic* duty.
She's active in several *civic* organizations.
The school teaches *civic* responsibility.

senses.gloss: Relating to a town or city and its public life.
examples: The concert is at the *civic* center.
The new park is a source of *civic* pride.

position: both — but *civil* meaning 'of citizens' or 'in law' goes only before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more civil*, *most civil* in the 'polite' sense; the other senses are not gradable
contrast: *Civil* and *civic* both translate as *гражданский*: *civil rights*, *civil war* and *a civil ceremony* are about citizens as opposed to the army or the church, while *civic duty* is about taking part in public life. *Civilian clothes* (not *civil clothes*) are clothes that are not a uniform.

senses.gloss: Relating to ordinary citizens and their rights, not to the military or religion.
examples: Martin Luther King Jr. was a leader of the *civil* rights movement.
The country was torn apart by *civil* war.
They had a *civil* ceremony at city hall instead of a church wedding.

senses.gloss: In law: about private disputes between people or companies, not about crimes.
examples: She filed a *civil* lawsuit against the company.
It's a *civil* case, so nobody is going to prison.

senses.gloss: Polite, but not especially friendly.
examples: Try to stay *civil* even if he gets angry.
They're divorced, but they're *civil* to each other.
The debate was more *civil* than anyone expected.

contrast: Usually a noun (*Two civilians were hurt*). The adjective goes before a noun: *civilian clothes*, *civilian life*; not *civil clothes*.

senses.gloss: Not belonging to the armed forces or the police.
examples: He found it hard to adjust to *civilian* life after the Army.
The bombing caused heavy *civilian* casualties.
The officers were in *civilian* clothes.

contrast: American spelling uses *z*: *civilized*, not *civilised*.

senses.gloss: Of a society: having an advanced system of laws, government and culture.
examples: Torture has no place in a *civilized* society.
Every *civilized* nation has laws against slavery.

senses.gloss: Polite, calm and reasonable; also pleasant and comfortable.
examples: Let's discuss this like *civilized* adults.
Dinner at eight is a much more *civilized* hour than dinner at five.
The divorce was surprisingly *civilized*.

position: predicative only — or right after a noun: *a woman clad in black*; before a noun only in compounds like *ivy-clad*

senses.gloss: Dressed in something, or covered with something.
examples: She was *clad* in a long red coat.
Two men *clad* in black stood by the door.
The building is *clad* in glass and steel.

contrast: Also a noun: *a clairvoyant*. Often used as a joke about someone who guesses well.

senses.gloss: Able to see the future or know things beyond the normal senses.
examples: She claims to have *clairvoyant* powers.
I'm not *clairvoyant* — you have to tell me what's wrong.
He said a *clairvoyant* dream warned him about the crash.

ru: липкий и влажный, холодный и потный

senses.gloss: Unpleasantly damp and sticky, and usually cold.
examples: My hands get *clammy* when I'm nervous.
The basement air was cold and *clammy*.
His forehead felt *clammier* by the minute.

senses.gloss: Done secretly, often because it is illegal or not allowed.
examples: They had a *clandestine* meeting in a parking garage.
The agency ran *clandestine* operations overseas.
Their affair stayed *clandestine* for years.

position: both — but the cosmetics sense only before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more clarifying* in the first sense

senses.gloss: Making something easier to understand.
examples: Can I ask a *clarifying* question?
The lawyer issued a *clarifying* statement.
Talking it through with my sister was really *clarifying*.

senses.gloss: Of a beauty product: removing oil and buildup.
examples: Use a *clarifying* shampoo once a week.
This *clarifying* toner works well on oily skin.

senses.gloss: Very aware of social class and of differences between classes.
senses.ru: с классовым сознанием; остро чувствующий социальные различия
examples: Victorian England was a deeply *class-conscious* society.
My grandmother was very *class-conscious*.
Americans are more *class-conscious* than they like to admit.

position: both — but *classified* ads only before a noun

senses.gloss: Officially secret and available only to certain people.
examples: He was charged with leaking *classified* documents.
I'm sorry, that information is *classified*.
The full report remains *classified*.

senses.gloss: Of ads: short, private and arranged by subject in a newspaper or on a website.
examples: She found her first apartment in the *classified* ads.
He sold his old truck through the *classified* section.

comparison: not gradable — but informally *totally classless* in the 'rude' sense

senses.gloss: Without divisions between social classes.
examples: Marx imagined a *classless* society.
America likes to see itself as *classless*, but it isn't.

senses.gloss: Informal: rude and lacking good manners, especially in sports.
examples: Mocking the injured player was a *classless* move.
The fans' behavior was totally *classless*.

senses.gloss: Stylish and expensive-looking; elegant.
examples: They went to a *classy* restaurant for their anniversary.
That dress is really *classy*.
It's the *classiest* hotel in town.

senses.gloss: Behaving with dignity and good manners.
examples: It was *classy* of him to congratulate the winner.
She handled the criticism in a very *classy* way.

senses.gloss: Afraid of being in small or crowded spaces.
examples: I get *claustrophobic* in elevators.
She's too *claustrophobic* to have an MRI.

senses.gloss: Of a place or situation: making you feel shut in.
examples: The apartment was dark and *claustrophobic*.
Living with my parents again felt *claustrophobic*.
The basement office is even more *claustrophobic* than the old one.

contrast: In *I clean forgot* and *The bullet went clean through*, *clean* is an informal adverb meaning 'completely'. Russian *чистый* in *чистый вес* or *чистая прибыль* is *net* in English: *net weight*, *net profit*, never *clean*.

senses.gloss: Not dirty.
examples: Are these towels *clean*?
Put on a *clean* shirt before dinner.
The kitchen is *cleaner* than it's been in weeks.

senses.gloss: Not causing or containing pollution.
examples: The state is investing in *clean* energy.
Everyone has a right to *clean* drinking water.
Electric buses are *cleaner* than diesel ones.

senses.gloss: Free of crimes, drugs or anything wrong.
examples: He has a *clean* driving record.
She's been *clean* for three years.
The athlete's drug test came back *clean*.

senses.gloss: Not offensive or sexual.
examples: Keep your jokes *clean* — there are kids here.
It's a *clean* comedy the whole family can watch.

senses.gloss: Smooth, simple and neat, with no rough or extra parts.
examples: I like the *clean* lines of modern furniture.
It was a *clean* break, so the bone should heal quickly.
The surgeon made a small, *clean* cut.

senses.gloss: Fair and played by the rules.
examples: It was a hard but *clean* game.
Both candidates promised to run a *clean* campaign.

contrast: Do not confuse it with *clear-cut*, which means definite or obvious (*a clear-cut case*).

senses.gloss: Neat, tidy and respectable-looking, often with short hair.
examples: He looked like a *clean-cut* college kid.
The candidate's *clean-cut* image helped him with older voters.
The band looked more *clean-cut* back in the '60s.

senses.gloss: With no beard or mustache.
examples: He showed up *clean-shaven* for the interview.
The suspect is a tall, *clean-shaven* man in his thirties.
Most of the players are *clean-shaven*.

position: both — but the skin-care sense only before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more cleansing* in the emotional sense
contrast: The vowel is short, as in *cleanse*: KLEN-zing, not KLEEN as in *clean*.

senses.gloss: Used to clean the skin or body.
examples: Wash your face with a gentle *cleansing* lotion.
She uses *cleansing* wipes to take off her makeup.

senses.gloss: Making you feel emotionally fresh and free of bad feelings.
examples: Take a deep, *cleansing* breath.
Crying can be very *cleansing*.
Finally telling the truth felt *cleansing*.

contrast: Compare *clean-cut*, which means neat and respectable-looking. The verb *clear-cut* means to cut down every tree in an area.

senses.gloss: Definite and easy to see or decide; not in doubt.
examples: It's not a *clear-cut* case of fraud.
The rules are *clear-cut*.
The answer was less *clear-cut* than we hoped.

senses.gloss: Seeing a situation clearly and realistically, without illusions.
examples: We need a *clear-eyed* look at the budget.
She's *clear-eyed* about the risks of starting a business.
Her book offers a *clear-eyed* view of the war.

contrast: Also spelled *clear-headed*.

senses.gloss: Able to think clearly and sensibly, especially when not tired, drunk or upset.
examples: I need to be *clearheaded* for the exam tomorrow.
She stayed calm and *clearheaded* during the emergency.
I feel more *clearheaded* in the morning.

senses.gloss: Of fists, teeth or a jaw: pressed together tightly, usually from anger or effort.
examples: He answered through *clenched* teeth.
She stood there with *clenched* fists.
His jaw was *clenched* the whole meeting.

form: -al; related to both *clerk* (office sense) and *cleric* (church sense)

senses.gloss: Relating to office work such as typing, filing and keeping records.
examples: She took a *clerical* job at the hospital.
The mistake was just a *clerical* error.
We need more *clerical* staff.

senses.gloss: Relating to priests and ministers.
examples: The priest wore a *clerical* collar.
The law was opposed by *clerical* leaders.

contrast: Also written *clichéd*. The stress is on the last syllable: klee-SHAYD.

senses.gloss: Used so often that it has become boring and unoriginal.
examples: The movie's ending was predictable and *cliched*.
Avoid *cliched* phrases like 'think outside the box.'
It sounds *cliched*, but money can't buy happiness.

contrast: Do not confuse it with *climatic*, which is about climate. *Climactic* has a *c* before the *t*, like *climax*.

senses.gloss: Forming the most exciting or important point of a story or event.
examples: In the *climactic* scene, the hero finally faces his father.
The *climactic* battle takes up the last hour of the movie.
The final game of the series was truly *climactic*.

position: both — but the medical sense mostly before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more clinical* in the 'cold' and 'bare' senses; the medical sense is not gradable
contrast: About a person, a style or a room, *clinical* is usually criticism: cold and without feeling. It is not an intensifier like Russian *клинический* in *клинический идиот*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the examination and treatment of patients, not to theory or lab work.
examples: The drug is still in *clinical* trials.
She has twenty years of *clinical* experience as a nurse.
He was diagnosed with *clinical* depression.

senses.gloss: Cold and without emotion; efficient but unfeeling.
examples: She described the accident in a calm, *clinical* way.
The team finished the game with *clinical* efficiency.
His writing is a little too *clinical* for my taste.

senses.gloss: Of a room or building: plain, very clean and unwelcoming, like a hospital.
examples: The new office feels cold and *clinical*.
They painted over the *clinical* white walls with a warm yellow.

contrast: Also a noun: *a pair of clip-ons*.

senses.gloss: Attached with a clip rather than pinned, tied or put through a hole.
examples: She wears *clip-on* earrings because her ears aren't pierced.
He showed up to the wedding in a *clip-on* tie.
I bought a *clip-on* reading light for my book.

senses.gloss: Of speech: short, quick and unfriendly.
examples: She answered in a *clipped* voice.
His replies grew more *clipped* as the interview went on.
The officer spoke in short, *clipped* sentences.

senses.gloss: Cut short and neat.
examples: The house has a neatly *clipped* hedge.
He has a *clipped* gray mustache.

senses.gloss: Forming small, closed groups that do not welcome outsiders.
examples: The kids at her new school were really *cliquish*.
It's a *cliquish* industry where everyone knows everyone.
The office got more *cliquish* after the merger.

senses.gloss: Involving secret, mysterious actions, like a spy story.
examples: The meeting had a *cloak-and-dagger* feel to it.
Why all the *cloak-and-dagger* stuff? Just tell me.
The whole deal was very *cloak-and-dagger*.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the adverb: *Turn it clockwise*
contrast: The adverb is more common than the adjective: *Turn the lid clockwise*. American English says *counterclockwise*; *anticlockwise* is British.

senses.gloss: Moving in the same direction as the hands of a clock.
examples: Stir the sauce in a *clockwise* direction.
The dancers moved in a slow *clockwise* circle.
Most screws tighten with a *clockwise* turn.

senses.gloss: Blocked so that liquid, air or traffic cannot move through easily.
examples: The kitchen sink is *clogged* again.
The highway was *clogged* with holiday traffic.
Plaque can lead to *clogged* arteries.

position: both — but *close* meaning careful or narrow usually goes before a noun: *a close look*, *a close call*
contrast: The adjective ends in an /s/ sound (KLOHS); the verb *close*, meaning shut, ends in /z/ (KLOHZ). *Close* is also an adverb (*Come close*; *They live close by*). For people, use *close*, not *near*: *a close friend*, never *a near friend*.

senses.gloss: Near in space or time.
examples: The hotel is *close* to the beach.
Christmas is getting *close*.
Where's the *closest* gas station?

senses.gloss: Knowing and liking each other very well.
examples: She's my *closest* friend.
I'm very *close* to my brother.
They have a *close* relationship.

senses.gloss: Directly related in a family.
examples: Only *close* relatives were invited to the funeral.
Her *closest* living relative is a cousin in Texas.

senses.gloss: Won or lost by a very small difference.
examples: It was a *close* game until the last minute.
The election is too *close* to call.
This year's race was *closer* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Careful and thorough.
examples: Take a *close* look at the contract before you sign.
Pay *close* attention to the instructions.

senses.gloss: Very similar.
examples: There's a *close* resemblance between the two sisters.
The translation is very *close* to the original.

senses.gloss: Almost happening, especially about something bad.
examples: Wow, that was *close* — that truck almost hit us!
We made our flight, but it was a *close* call.

senses.gloss: Of a group: whose members know, help and care about each other.
examples: We grew up in a *close-knit* neighborhood.
Her family is very *close-knit*.
Small towns tend to be more *close-knit* than big cities.

comparison: not gradable — but *more closed* or *very closed* when it means not open to people or ideas
contrast: A store that is not open is *closed*, not *close*: *The bank is closed on Sundays*. *Close* (KLOHS) is a different adjective meaning near.

senses.gloss: Not open; shut, or not doing business.
examples: Keep the windows *closed* — it's freezing.
Sorry, we're *closed*.
The road is *closed* for repairs.

senses.gloss: Not open to outsiders or to new ideas.
examples: The hearing was *closed* to the public.
It's a very *closed* community.
He has a *closed* mind when it comes to politics.

senses.gloss: Finished and no longer being discussed or investigated.
examples: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is *closed*.
Police say the case is now *closed*.

senses.gloss: Of a TV show or video: with words on the screen that can be turned on for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
examples: This program is *closed-captioned* for viewers who are deaf or hard of hearing.
All of our training videos are *closed-captioned*.
Look for the CC symbol on *closed-captioned* shows.

contrast: British *CCTV* is usually *security cameras* or *surveillance cameras* in everyday American speech.

senses.gloss: Of TV or video: sent only to certain screens, not broadcast to the public.
examples: The store is monitored by *closed-circuit* cameras.
The fight was shown on *closed-circuit* TV in theaters.
Police reviewed the *closed-circuit* footage.

contrast: After a verb, say *behind closed doors*: *The talks were held behind closed doors*.

senses.gloss: Held in private, without the public or reporters.
examples: Senators met in a *closed-door* session.
The deal was made during *closed-door* negotiations.
The committee held a *closed-door* hearing on the leak.

senses.gloss: Coming at the end of something.
examples: The lawyer gave a powerful *closing* argument.
They scored twice in the *closing* minutes.
The stock's *closing* price was $42.

contrast: Everyday English says *dressed* (*Get dressed*). *Clothed* is more formal and common in *fully clothed*.

senses.gloss: Wearing clothes.
examples: He fell asleep fully *clothed*.
The children were poorly fed and poorly *clothed*.
She was *clothed* in a white robe.

senses.gloss: Of thinking or judgment: confused or affected by a strong feeling.
examples: His judgment was *clouded* by anger.
For weeks, her mind was *clouded* with grief.

senses.gloss: Not clear or bright; also made less certain or less happy.
examples: The bathroom has a *clouded* glass window.
Her eyes were *clouded* with tears.
The future of the project is *clouded* by money problems.

senses.gloss: With no clouds.
examples: It was a warm day with a *cloudless* blue sky.
The sky over the desert was *cloudless*.
We watched the stars on a *cloudless* night.

senses.gloss: Of the sky or weather: full of clouds.
examples: It's *cloudy* but not raining.
Expect a *cloudy* morning with sun later.
Seattle is much *cloudier* than Los Angeles.

senses.gloss: Of a liquid or glass: not clear.
examples: The water in the pool looks *cloudy*.
Throw out the medicine if it turns *cloudy*.

senses.gloss: Silly and foolish, like a clown.
examples: His *clownish* behavior annoyed the teacher.
The senator's *clownish* antics made headlines.
Critics called the performance *clownish*.

senses.gloss: Too sweet or too sentimental, in an unpleasant way.
examples: The frosting was so sweet it was *cloying*.
The movie's *cloying* ending made me roll my eyes.
His letters got more *cloying* over time.

senses.gloss: Knowing nothing about something; not understanding what is going on.
examples: I'm totally *clueless* about cars.
The new manager seems *clueless*.
He gave me a *clueless* look.

senses.gloss: Moving awkwardly and often dropping or breaking things.
examples: I'm so *clumsy* — I just spilled coffee on my laptop.
The puppy is still *clumsy* on its feet.
He's the *clumsiest* person I know.

senses.gloss: Done without skill or tact.
examples: He made a *clumsy* attempt at an apology.
The translation is *clumsy* in places.

senses.gloss: Awkward to use or carry because of its size or shape.
examples: The first cell phones were big and *clumsy*.
Firefighters used to wear heavy, *clumsy* gear.

senses.gloss: Heavy, awkward and badly designed; not smooth or elegant.
examples: She wore *clunky* black boots.
The old software is slow and *clunky*.
The dialogue in the second book is even *clunkier*.

senses.gloss: Grouped closely together.
examples: A few houses sit *clustered* around the church.
Most of the restaurants are *clustered* near the waterfront.
From the hill we could see the *clustered* tents of the camp.

senses.gloss: Full of too many things, in an untidy way.
examples: His desk is always *cluttered* with papers.
The *cluttered* garage hadn't been cleaned in years.
The website's home page is too *cluttered*.

contrast: Often written *coed*. The noun *a coed*, meaning a female college student, is old-fashioned and now sounds sexist.

senses.gloss: For both male and female students or members.
examples: She went to a *co-ed* boarding school.
The dorms on campus are *co-ed*.
We play in a *co-ed* softball league.

senses.gloss: Producing heat or power by burning coal.
examples: The state plans to close its last *coal-fired* power plant.
*Coal-fired* plants are a major source of carbon emissions.
The old ship had a *coal-fired* engine.

contrast: It sounds exactly like *course* (*of course*, *a college course*).

senses.gloss: Rough to touch, or made of large grains or thick threads.
examples: The dog has *coarse* black fur.
Sprinkle the steak with *coarse* salt.
Start with *coarser* sandpaper, then switch to a fine one.

senses.gloss: Rude and offensive, especially about sex or the body.
examples: He has a *coarse* sense of humor.
Her language got pretty *coarse* after a few drinks.

senses.gloss: On or near a coast.
examples: They live in a small *coastal* town in Maine.
*Coastal* areas face a growing risk of flooding.
Most of the state's population is *coastal*.

senses.gloss: Covered with a thin layer of something.
examples: The car was *coated* in dust.
These pills are *coated* so they're easier to swallow.
She bought a bag of *chocolate-coated* almonds.

contrast: American slang; also spelled *cockamamy*.

senses.gloss: Silly, crazy and hard to believe.
examples: Where did you get that *cockamamie* idea?
He told some *cockamamie* story about losing his keys in a lake.
It was the most *cockamamie* plan I'd ever heard.

senses.gloss: Crooked; not straight or level.
examples: The picture on the wall is *cockeyed*.
He wore his cap at a *cockeyed* angle.

senses.gloss: Silly and not sensible.
examples: That's the most *cockeyed* plan I've ever heard.
He has some *cockeyed* theory about the moon landing.

senses.gloss: Too confident, in a way that annoys people.
examples: He was young and *cocksure* and thought he knew everything.
Her *cocksure* attitude cost her the job.
Don't get *cocksure* just because you won one game.

senses.gloss: Too confident and proud of yourself, in a way that annoys people.
examples: He got a little *cocky* after his first big win.
Don't be so *cocky* — the season just started.
He's the *cockiest* guy on the team.

senses.gloss: Written down as a formal set of rules or laws.
examples: The right is *codified* in federal law.
The company has no *codified* dress code.
Many of these customs were never *codified*.

contrast: In everyday speech Americans say *co-ed* or *coed*.

senses.gloss: Of a school or college: for both male and female students.
examples: Yale College became *coeducational* in 1969.
It is one of the oldest *coeducational* colleges in the country.
The academy runs a *coeducational* summer program.

senses.gloss: Using force or threats to make people do things.
examples: The police were accused of using *coercive* interrogation methods.
Critics say the policy is *coercive*.
*Coercive* control is a form of domestic abuse.

senses.gloss: Clear, logical and convincing.
examples: She made a *cogent* argument for raising taxes.
His reasons were *cogent* and well researched.
I've never heard a more *cogent* explanation of the problem.

senses.gloss: Relating to thinking, learning, memory and understanding.
examples: The disease slowly affects *cognitive* function.
Reading aloud helps children's *cognitive* development.
She's a researcher in *cognitive* psychology.

contrast: Formal. In everyday English say *aware of*.

senses.gloss: Knowing about something; aware.
examples: We are *cognizant* of the risks.
Employees must be *cognizant* of the new safety rules.
Parents need to be more *cognizant* of what their kids see online.

senses.gloss: Logical, clear and well organized.
examples: We need a *coherent* plan for the next five years.
Her essay was clear and *coherent*.
The second draft is much more *coherent*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: able to speak clearly and sensibly.
examples: He was so tired he was barely *coherent*.
By the time the ambulance came, she was *coherent* again.
